rv.q: Anne Kauffman's wonderful revival for the Roundabout Theatre Company, giving the play its overdue Broadway debut
Strongly dappled as it is by images of illness and mortality, “Marvin’s Room” still shines with vital, quirky life.
Anne Kauffman's luminous revival for the Roundabout tends to McPherson's legacy with grace.
But it is somehow, also, fatally mild.
'Marvin's Room' is a thickly sugared pill, glib and sentimental to a fault.

A cute sense of humor pops up throughout the play, such as when Ruth dresses up for a special episode of her favorite television soap opera, Lee shamelessly dumps a tray of candy into her purse while touring a nursing home and Bessie is rescued at Disney World by a costumed cartoon character.
A play that resonated deeply back in its day ends up now gasping for oxygen on a stage full of dead air.
Under the direction of Anne Kauffman it's given a fairly ho-hum Broadway debut.
Unfortunately, this first Broadway production of Marvin’s Roomnever quite justifies its trip back to the early ’90s.

The new Broadway revival, now playing at the Theatre and superbly directed by Anne Kauffman, does "Marvin's Room" extraordinary justice -- it makes the case that a mostly forgotten play might just be a modern classic.
A work that could have succumbed to all sorts of excess miraculously never puts a foot wrong.
Zany, morbid, and brimful of compassion, Marvin’s Room is the defining work of a playwright who died of complications from AIDS at the age of 33.
Lili Taylor's naturalistic performance is downright life-affirming.
Taylor is the rare actor who seems to shrug off her charisma while never actually letting it go.
“Marvin’s Room” is at its finest when reminding us that memory is a fierce, potent counterpoint to fear of the unknown.
All the choices in this tender revival reveal an involving and human story, unmarred by overdrawn theatrics.
She steers the uniformly credible cast through a sometimes flighty comedy ultimately grounded in compassion.
The brief candle of his great talent shines in the belated Broadway premiere of Marvin's Room, notwithstanding the design and staging miscalculation noted here.
Marvin’s Room will be a rewarding place to be this summer.
Even if all the comic business still landed throughout instead of rather sporadically, it's not as a comedy that Marvin's Room survives but as a very human look at life, love and death.
While the acting is fine, the comedic elements of the story about the intertwining of life and death sometimes feel forced.
In the end, despite the incongruities between the production and the play itself, Marvin's Room resonates with beautiful insights into the ways we approach the end of life.
It almost makes you forget how disappointing this current revival of an otherwise moving play is.
While it may have augured well for its creator, who died in 1992 at age 33 after receiving several major awards, it seems to have lost much of its vigor in the intervening decades.
McPherson whimsically juggles the real and the unreal, the sick and the inane.
I deeply admire how it becomes demystified here, returned to the realm of the mundane and the slightly funny, where it always belonged.
On close inspection, McPherson’s play delivers a defiantly positive prognoses.
Overall, this is a great cast taking on a 'pretty good' play.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this Broadway debut, with critics divided on whether McPherson's 1991 play still resonates. Strong performances from Taylor, Garofalo, and Weston praised, but many find the pacing sluggish and material dated.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
